headline: Organigram and Aurora file merger circular, set 23 December votes
dek: Organigram and Aurora Cannabis filed their joint circular on 25 November, setting back-to-back votes on 23 December, 19 days after Curaleaf's rival bid expires.
key_points: Organigram and Aurora Cannabis filed their joint management information circular on 25 November for the C$7.80-a-share deal announced on 3 November.
Both companies will hold virtual special meetings on 23 December, Organigram at 9:00 a.m. and Aurora at 9:30 a.m. Eastern, with proxies due on 21 December.
Aurora holders would own roughly 35% to 37% of the combined company's economic interest, depending on the source, and about 41% to 42% of the votes.
Curaleaf's competing offer still expires on 4 December unless extended, leaving a 19-day gap before Aurora shareholders vote.
body: Organigram and Aurora Cannabis have filed the joint management information circular for their merger, moving the deal from announcement to shareholder vote. The companies said on 25 November that the document, which sets out the terms and the case for the transaction, has been filed in support of the arrangement agreement that would bring Aurora under Organigram's ownership.

Both companies will vote on the same day. According to The Marijuana Herald's account of the circular, Organigram holds its special meeting at 9:00 a.m. Eastern on 23 December and Aurora at 9:30 a.m., both online, with proxies due by the matching times on 21 December. Completion is still targeted for January 2027, subject to shareholder, court and regulatory approvals, including clearances in Canada and Germany.

The terms are unchanged from the 3 November announcement. Aurora shareholders can choose C$7.80 in cash per share, 5.8626 Organigram shares, or a mix of C$3.75 in cash plus 3.0431 Organigram shares. Elections for all cash or all stock are prorated against two caps set out in the original release: 205,826,172 Organigram shares and C$253,638,772 in cash. As we reported on 6 November, the deal values Aurora at about C$561 million.

Those caps say a lot about the deal's shape. On our arithmetic, the cash cap is about 45% of the C$561 million headline value, so shareholders who all ask for cash will receive a blend. The companies describe the offer as a 93% premium to Aurora's unaffected share price before Curaleaf's unsolicited bid, and the Herald reports the circular puts it 21% above the implied value of Curaleaf's offer as of 2 November.
Both boards unanimously recommend the deal. Aurora's board and its independent special committee have twice found Curaleaf's competing offer financially inadequate, according to the Herald.
> The circular turns a bidding war into a calendar. Curaleaf's offer lapses on 4 December; the vote that decides Aurora's future comes 19 days later.

The ownership split is one detail that has shifted between documents. The 3 November release said Aurora shareholders would hold about 35% of the combined company's economic interest and 42% of its voting interest on a fully diluted basis. The Herald, summarising the circular, reports about 37% economic and 41% voting. We have not been able to read the circular itself to reconcile the two; the difference may reflect updated share counts.

The cash side is funded from existing cash, credit facilities from ATB Financial of up to C$210 million, and a private placement in which British American Tobacco, already a strategic shareholder in Organigram, buys 141.0 million Organigram shares at C$1.33 for gross proceeds of about C$187.5 million. Above a 30% threshold, BAT receives non-voting preferred shares instead of common shares.
## What the combined company would be

The pitch is international medical cannabis. The companies say the combined business would have leading positions in Canada, Germany, Poland, Australia and New Zealand, about 170,000 kilograms of annual cultivation capacity, and 14 production, research and distribution facilities, five of them EU-GMP certified. They expect more than C$50 million a year in synergies from distribution, purchasing, cross-selling and lower operating costs, and say most combined revenue would come from international medical markets. The Herald's account does not name the combined company or its leadership, and we have not seen either in the documents we read.

Aurora needs at least two-thirds of the votes cast at its meeting, plus a simple majority excluding votes that must be set aside under the Canadian minority-protection rule MI 61-101. Organigram needs a simple majority of votes cast, excluding BAT's shares, because BAT is a party to the financing. The record date for Aurora's meeting was 18 November, according to a notice filed with the SEC that we covered on 10 November.

Curaleaf's hostile offer of US$1 in cash plus 0.4013 Curaleaf shares per Aurora share was due to expire on 4 December unless extended, as we reported on 10 and 12 November. Curaleaf has already cleared competition reviews in Germany and Canada, the only two jurisdictions where its bid needed them. That leaves Curaleaf with three options before the vote: let its bid lapse, extend it, or improve it. The circular is designed to make the Organigram deal the default if it does none of the first two in a way shareholders prefer.

Watch 4 December for any Curaleaf extension or improved terms. Watch for proxy adviser recommendations on both votes in mid-December, and for an interim court order under the arrangement process. Proxies close on 21 December and both meetings are on 23 December. If shareholders approve, the remaining steps are the final court order and regulatory clearances in Canada and Germany, with closing targeted for January 2027.
